messages.author: b898ede89d0342de
messages.subject: Pseudoreplication in population RSF analysis
parts:
Hello Group,

 

I am currently in the process of formalizing the methods I am going to use for a population based RSF analysis for raptors in Alaska during the summer. About half of the individuals have data which spans multiple years, with individuals returning to the same general area each year. A quick 100% MCP for a few birds that returned multiple years shows substantial overlap for each individual.

My question that I am putting to the group are which methods are used to mitigate pseudoreplication that would arise when including data from multiple years from the same individual?

 I know in Alston et al. 2023 it is said that the weighting based on the effective sample size can account for individuals having different time scales but some of my individuals have returned for 3 consecutive years with each year having an effective sample size of 250+. I am concerned that these individuals might pull a population level analysis to their habitat selection  if I treat each year as a “new” individual (ex. hawk X 2021, hawk X 2022, hawk X 2023, hawk Y 2022, hawk Z 2023).

Possible methods I have thought of were:

  1. Using the mean function and getting a mean for all the years that an individual was present and then putting that into the population mean for the population analysis.
  2. Randomly select a year from the multiple ones and just using that for the analysis.
  3. Go forward with counting each year as an independent individual.

Thank you in advance for any insights anyone might be able to give!

-Jonah

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Pseudoreplication in population RSF analysis
parts:
Hi Jonah,

If they are using the same general area, then you can just treat that all as one individual track and estimate one individual RSF with those years.
If they were using different areas, then I think you could run those years through mean() first and then include that with the other individuals in the population mean.

Best,
Chris
